text: Color and style, driven directly by the data itself instead of set by hand, one cell or one bar at a time. Three ways to do it, and we'll go through all three, starting with the most common.

Rules let you assign a color to specific value ranges you define yourself — green above a target, yellow near it, red below it. Set each range as a percent of the overall min-to-max spread, or as a literal number instead — mixing those two settings up is genuinely the single most common conditional formatting mistake people make, so double-check which one your rule actually needs before moving on.

Data bars turn each table cell into a tiny bar chart of its own — longer bar, higher value, readable at a glance without leaving the table at all. Toggle Show bar only to hide the number entirely and let the bar speak for itself.

Icons attach a small status symbol to each value instead — a diamond, a triangle, a circle, an arrow — grouped by category as Directional, Shapes, Indicators, and Ratings, readable at a glance with no legend required. And this same Gradient, Rules, and Field value logic works well beyond tables and matrices — column and bar charts, button slicers, and cards all support conditional formatting too.

A practical habit worth adopting: write a measure that returns the exact color you want directly, as a hex code, and apply it with Field value formatting — often faster to maintain than a pile of rules once your logic gets even slightly complex. Next: the Filters pane — every level a filter can apply at, from a single visual all the way up to the whole report.
